title: Bio-ML in 2026: AlphaFold 3, ESM-3, and the protein-foundation-model frontier
summary: Where bio-ML stands after the AlphaFold breakthrough. Multimodal protein foundation models (ESM-3) now rival AlphaFold while adding generative capability. Single-cell foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT) are emerging. Where each stands, where the gaps are, what's next.
abstract: The 2020 AlphaFold breakthrough effectively solved protein structure prediction. The years since have seen the field broaden: AlphaFold 3 extends to multi-molecule complexes; ESM-3 adds multimodal sequence + structure + function modeling with generative capability; single-cell foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT, UCE) bring transformer pretraining to scRNA-seq. Bio-ML benchmarks remain a perpetual challenge — homology leakage is endemic; only CASP-style time-based + sequence-similarity-stratified splits keep the field honest. This paper surveys the 2026 state of bio-ML across protein, single-cell, and emerging modalities, with practical recommendations.
contentIntro:
## What's covered

Three dominant fronts of bio-ML in 2026:

- **Protein structure** (AlphaFold 2/3, ESMFold)
- **Protein language models** (ESM-2/3, ProGen, ProstT5)
- **Single-cell foundation models** (Geneformer, scGPT, UCE)

This paper covers the state-of-the-art in each, the empirical trade-offs, and where the field is heading.

## Protein structure prediction

**AlphaFold 2 (2020)**: median GDT_TS ~92 on CASP14. Effectively solved single-chain protein folding.

**AlphaFold-Multimer (2021)**: extended to protein-protein complexes. Significant improvement on heterodimers and homooligomers.

**AlphaFold 3 (2024)**: multimodal complexes — protein-protein, protein-ligand, protein-DNA, protein-RNA. Diffusion-based structure module replacing IPA. New SOTA across most multimer benchmarks.

**ESMFold (2022)**: ESM-2 + small structure module. ~85 GDT_TS without using MSAs at all. Faster than AlphaFold (no MSA search). Trade-off: ~7 points of accuracy for ~10× speed.

**State of the art**:
- For single-chain, well-aligned proteins: AlphaFold 2 or 3.
- For complexes: AlphaFold 3.
- For high-throughput screens: ESMFold (faster, MSA-free).
- For orphan proteins (no homologs): ESMFold often matches AlphaFold.

## Protein language models

**ESM-1/2 (2019-2022)**: BERT-style. UniRef pretraining. Released sizes from 8M to 15B params. Standard for embedding extraction + variant effect prediction.

**ESM-3 (2024)**: multimodal — sequence + structure + function tokens. ~98B params. Generative; can design novel proteins. Used to design esmGFP (a fluorescent protein with no natural homolog).

**ProGen, ProtGPT2**: autoregressive generative pLMs. Sample new sequences with desired properties.

**ProstT5**: structure-aware. Pretrained on sequence + structure jointly.

**Domain-specific pLMs**: AbLang (antibodies), CARP (CRISPR proteins), various enzyme-specific models. Smaller, faster, more accurate within domain.

## Single-cell foundation models

**scVI (2018)**: VAE with biology-aware likelihood. The standard tool for scRNA-seq embedding + batch correction. Not a 'foundation model' in the modern sense but the workhorse.

**Geneformer (2023)**: transformer trained on 30M cells via masked-token prediction (where tokens are gene-rank sequences). ~30M params. Embeds cells; fine-tunable for downstream tasks.

**scGPT (2023)**: GPT-style; autoregressive on cells.

**UCE (2023)**: Universal Cell Embeddings; trained across many species.

State-of-the-art is more diffuse here than in protein. Different models excel on different downstream tasks; no single 'best' yet.

## Multi-modal extensions

- **Spatial transcriptomics** (STAGATE, GraphST): scRNA-seq + spatial coordinates.
- **Multi-omics integration**: RNA + ATAC + protein + perturbation. totalVI, MOFA+, CrossVAE.
- **Causal/perturbation prediction**: predict cell-state changes from interventions. CellOracle, perturbational atlases.

## Where bio-ML still struggles

**Protein design at scale**: ESM-3 can design novel proteins, but the success rate (designed protein actually folds + has the desired function) is still ~10-30%. For practical use, design + experimental screening is the production loop. Pure-design without experiment is research-stage.

**Disordered proteins**: ~30% of human proteins have significant disorder. AlphaFold gives low pLDDT in these regions; predictions aren't really meaningful. ESM gives embeddings but no structure. Conformational ensembles are needed; MD + ML hybrid approaches are emerging.

**Membrane proteins**: trained mostly on soluble proteins. Membrane-embedded geometry is harder. AlphaFold 3 improves; still not at full parity with soluble proteins.

**Long context for genomics**: standard transformers are O(N²); genomic sequences are millions of bases. HyenaDNA (Caduceus, etc.) push to 100K+ tokens via state-space models. Still not full-genome context.

**Low-resource species**: bio-ML methods perform best on well-studied species (human, mouse, model organisms). Coverage of bacterial, archaeal, viral diversity is uneven. Foundation models trained on broader databases (UniRef vs UniRef50) help.

**Experimental validation**: bio-ML predictions need experimental validation for high-stakes use (therapeutics, agriculture). The 'predict in silico, validate in vitro' loop is the standard; pure prediction without wet-lab follow-up isn't trustworthy.

## Benchmarks: a perpetual challenge

**The leakage problem**: protein sequence databases are redundant. Random train/test splits cause homology leakage. Methods 'beat the SOTA' on leaky benchmarks but fail on truly held-out data.

**Solutions**:

1. **Sequence-similarity-restricted splits** (30% identity cutoff): standard for serious bio-ML benchmarks. TAPE, ProteinNet, FLIP all use this.

2. **Time-based holdouts**: train on data before time T, test on later data. CASP's design.

3. **CATH/SCOP fold splits**: test set contains protein folds not in training. Strictest test of generalization; rarely used in practice.

**Currently-trustworthy benchmarks**:
- **CASP**: structure prediction. The gold standard.
- **ProteinGym**: variant effect prediction. Well-curated; deep mutational scanning data.
- **TAPE**: protein representation tasks. Sequence-similarity-stratified.
- **FLIP**: protein function landscape. Includes hard splits.

**Trust calibration**: a 5% improvement on a leaky benchmark might be 0% on a clean one. Always check the split methodology.

## Practical recommendations

For a team building bio-ML in 2026:

**Protein structure**:
- Single-chain, with MSA: AlphaFold 2.
- Multi-chain or with ligands: AlphaFold 3.
- High-throughput, MSA-free: ESMFold.
- Experimental validation when stakes are high.

**Protein representations**:
- Embedding extraction: ESM-2 650M (frozen) + downstream classifier. Standard pattern.
- Variant effect: ESM-1v or ESM-2 with log-likelihood ratio.
- Domain-specific (antibodies, etc.): use domain-specific pLM if available.

**Single-cell**:
- Standard pipeline: Scanpy + scVI for batch-corrected embeddings.
- Cell-type classification: CellTypist or fine-tuned Geneformer.
- Trajectory inference: PAGA + RNA velocity.
- Foundation models: emerging; benchmark on your specific task before relying.

**Generative protein design**:
- ESM-3 (via API).
- Structure-conditioned design: RFDiffusion, ProteinMPNN.
- Antibody design: specialized tools (RFdiffusion, IgLM, AbLang).
- Validate experimentally; success rate ~10-30%.

## Where the field is going

**Protein foundation models will dominate**. ESM-3-class multimodal models will be the unified backbone for protein structure, function, and design. Vendor-specific (Evolutionary Scale, Generate Biomedicines) and open-source (Meta AI, academic) variants.

**Single-cell foundation models will mature**. Right now there's not a clear 'BERT for cells'; multiple candidates (Geneformer, scGPT, UCE) compete. By 2027-2028, expect convergence on a dominant recipe.

**Multi-modal integration will be the central theme**. Bio-ML increasingly combines RNA + protein + structure + spatial + perturbation. Joint embedding models become the norm.

**Experimental + ML loops will tighten**. AI-driven experimental design (active learning, Bayesian optimization) + high-throughput experimentation (DMS, CRISPR screens) → faster iteration. The bio-ML workflow becomes 'predict → screen → re-train'.

**Benchmark rigor will improve**. The field is becoming aware of leakage; new benchmarks (CASP-class) are emerging across domains. Trust calibration improves.

For learners interested in bio-ML: the field is a few years behind language modeling in maturity but moving fast. The substrate (sequences, structures, single cells, dynamics) is well-defined; the methods are the same family as NLP/vision (transformers + scale). The biology-specific adaptations are what make it its own discipline. The combination of biology + scaling laws + frontier ML methods is one of the highest-leverage areas in science right now.

paperStructure.researchQuestion: What's the state of bio-ML in 2026? Where are the methods strong, where do gaps remain, what's the practical recommendation for new projects?
paperStructure.method: Survey of major architectures (AlphaFold 2/3, ESM-2/3, scVI, Geneformer, scGPT, UCE) on standard benchmarks (CASP, ProteinGym, TAPE, scRNA-seq atlases). Practical guidance for production use.
paperStructure.results: AlphaFold 2/3 dominate structure; ESM-3 leads multimodal protein foundation models; single-cell foundation models converging. Persistent gaps: disordered proteins, membrane proteins, long-context genomics, low-resource species. Benchmark rigor improving but homology leakage remains endemic.
